boundaries: a media route -> a browser's cache, and the middleware writing over it
the cache middleware -> every handler under /api/

instruments.evidence: One helper and its four call sites. The boundary is a browser's own cache: what a route says it may keep, and what the middleware says over the top of it.

Ledgers 68b74a58a, a053fc7eb and 121713a04, all of this media path. cache-R3 in the second was the same shape one layer up -- a header the client overrode -- and this is the same defect one layer down, where a middleware overrode the route.

instruments.why: No assembled string or provider payload changed.
No component changed. The tile was READ in the running app, and its markup is what led to the header work, but nothing in it was edited.

instruments.evidence: The whole finding. Printed the complete response rather than the four headers I expected, and Pragma: no-cache and Expires: 0 were sitting under the max-age. Printed again after the fix: both gone, Cache-Control intact.

instruments.why: No query, migration or stored row changed.

instruments.evidence: The three cache headers now agree on every media route rather than contradicting each other.
No shape crossing to a client changed; the headers around it did.

instruments.why: No rule lives in two implementations.

instruments.evidence: The other end is a browser's cache, and it was asked directly rather than reasoned about: force-cache served in 2ms while default took 141ms, which is a stored response that is never fresh.

instruments.why: No field added to a struct that crosses a boundary.

instruments.evidence: The measurement environment was the fixture, and it was wrong twice. A hidden pane makes every viewport-driven measurement lie -- lazy loading defers forever, IntersectionObserver never fires -- and I had drawn a whole conclusion from it before checking document.visibilityState. Every measurement in this pass was taken with visibility asserted.
Both real cases: a cacheable route clears the blanket headers, a no-store route keeps them.
The no-store routes must not become cacheable by accident, which is asserted rather than assumed.
The middleware's headers are set before the handler runs, so the test sets them the same way rather than trusting the handler to be reached in isolation.

The uploads handler already deleted both headers for exactly this reason. The media routes were the sibling that never got it -- and finding that is what made this a one-line fix rather than an investigation.
Both branches of the explore route reached, signed in and anonymous.
Nothing new is swallowed.
Nothing new is gated on a flag.
Four copies of a header pattern became one helper.
The shape is 'a middleware writes a header the handler also writes'. Grepped every Pragma and Expires in the tree: the middleware, the uploads fix, and now this. No fourth writer.
No transaction. The header write happens before the body, which is why it can be cleared at all.
One control, built after the commit, replayed by hand: both tests fail with named assertions.
The helper is the only way these routes set a cache lifetime now, so a future route cannot set max-age without clearing the blanket headers.
go build, go vet, gofmt clean. The handlers package passes with -p 1.
No new instrument. C7 earned its keep on the measurement environment rather than a code fixture, and that reading is now recorded in gotchas.md as well as here.

Applied in the sense that matters here: the running app, in a visible browser, timing the same thumbnail three ways before and after. 141ms default against 2ms force-cache before; 2 to 6ms default after; a second visit to Explore drawing its tile in 2ms with no request.

findings.summary: the cache middleware stamps Pragma: no-cache and Expires: 0 on every response under /api/, so a media route's own max-age was stored but never treated as fresh -- every visit revalidated and the entire caching change was decoration

control.observed: both FAIL: 'Pragma: no-cache outlived the max-age'
